fields.v: Dente, F., Satriani, D., Papotti, P. (2026). Constraint Decay: The Fragility of LLM Agents in Backend Code Generation. Published as a conference paper at COLM 2026 (Conference on Language Modeling). Read from arXiv:2605.06445v2 [cs.SE], 18 Sep 2026
Conference — COLM 2026 (Conference on Language Modeling) (header 'Published as a conference paper at COLM 2026'); full text read from arXiv:2605.06445v2
EURECOM, France (Dente, Papotti); University of Basilicata, Italy (Satriani). Academic; funded by EU Horizon Europe AI4SWEng (No. 101189909) and 3IA Côte d'Azur (ANR-23-IACL-0001)

Evaluates; secondary: Proposes an evaluation method — controlled study of how layered structural constraints (Clean Architecture, database engine, ORM) affect LLM agents generating a multi-file REST backend from a fixed OpenAPI contract (80 greenfield tasks over 8 frameworks, L0-L3), with 20 feature-implementation tasks, framework sensitivity and failure root-cause analysis; open-source evaluation pipeline with behavioral tests and static verifiers

No SDD approach named. Input format: OpenAPI 3.0 specification (RealWorld Conduit API) plus prompt constraint blocks. Scaffolds: Mini-SWE-Agent (instance prompt replaced with a 4-step generative workflow) and OpenHands (re-prompting wrapper against premature halting, up to 6 turns); versions Not stated. Models: Devstral-Small (24B), Qwen3-Coder-Next (80B), Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct, MiniMax-M2.5, Kimi-K2.5, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4

Per task (benchmark input): OpenAPI 3.0 YAML specification (~500 lines, 19 endpoints, 5 resource groups); structural constraint blocks (Clean Architecture with four layers routes/handlers, services/use cases, models/entities, repository/data access in separate directories with top-down dependencies; SQLite or PostgreSQL with schema created at startup; SQLAlchemy or Sequelize ORM); mandatory files requirements.txt/package.json and run.sh; server configuration (port, /api prefix, health-check); description of the evaluation pipeline

Not stated as a prescribed development flow. Mini-SWE-Agent injected workflow: analyze the codebase -> edit/create source code -> test edge cases -> submit. Evaluation pipeline: build phase (agent codes, builds, starts server in a container; patch extracted) -> evaluate phase (patch applied in a pristine container, server started, health-check polled, Postman/Newman suite run, static verifiers run)
None (fully automated runs, no manual intervention); one author manually labelled 50 failures to validate the LLM judge
N/A (no SDD approach); agents run end to end from a structured specification (OpenAPI) with varying structural constraints

Not classifiable; authors do not use SDD terms ('leveraging OpenAPI specifications as a structured way of expressing functional requirements', 'API-first development', 'evaluation methodology inspired by Behavior-Driven Development', 'rigorous adherence to structured specifications')
Both: new projects (80 greenfield generation tasks from an empty repository) and existing code bases (20 feature-implementation tasks re-implementing ablated features in RealWorld repositories)

One API contract: 19 CRUD endpoints, OpenAPI ~500 lines. 80 generation tasks = 8 frameworks x 10 constraint combinations (L0 8, L1 24, L2 32, L3 16); generated patches ~500-2,000 added lines. 20 feature tasks over 5 repositories (4 each), 161-2,604 lines removed across 2-46 files. Test suite: 32 requests, 291 assertions. Subset of 16 tasks for 3 configurations. ~4 billion tokens in total
Web backend REST API (RealWorld Conduit blogging platform: articles, comments, users, profiles, tags) in Python 3.12 (Flask, FastAPI, Django, aiohttp) and Node.js 20 (Express, Fastify, Hono, Koa)
N/A (autonomous agents, no human participants)
Token consumption: average and total input/output tokens per run by constraint level and per agent-model pair (Appendix I); cost limit left unbounded; no money or time reported

Assert% (A%): mean fraction of the 291 behavioral assertions passed across runs (zeroed when a structural verifier fails; also reported raw); pass@k (unbiased estimator; success = full behavioral suite passes and all applicable verifiers pass); pass@1 on feature tasks

Structural compliance by static verifiers: architecture (>=3 of 4 Clean Architecture layers, no upward imports), database engine evidence, ORM evidence (used as pass/fail gates, not reported separately)
None

Marginal effect of each constraint on A% via matched-pair differences (± stderr); A% by framework (± stderr) and best-to-worst spread; failure taxonomy (7 coarse categories, 6 logic-error root causes) for four Mini-SWE configurations; LLM-judge agreement (Cohen's kappa 0.975); subset-vs-full correlation (Pearson r 0.948, Spearman rho 0.932)

Automatic: Postman collection run with Newman against the server in a pristine Docker container (PostgreSQL 16 service); static regex verifiers on the added lines of the patch; token counts from runs. LLM-as-judge: GPT-5.2 (temperature 0) classifies failures from last 20 trajectory turns, test results, server logs and verifier outputs, validated by one author on 50 samples (98% accuracy)

Criterion (task level): run succeeds when the full behavioral suite passes and all applicable verifiers pass; no configuration-level threshold. n=3 trials per task; Mini-SWE-Agent max 300 iterations, OpenHands max 200; cost unbounded. For every configuration: quality: no criterion stated by the authors (authors call L3 results unreliable for production without a threshold); cost: no criterion stated by the authors

Project/tasks: one fixed OpenAPI contract (RealWorld Conduit) instantiated in 80 generation tasks (8 frameworks x 10 constraint combinations, L0 baseline to L3) plus 20 feature tasks. Configurations: 11 scaffold-model pairs (2 scaffolds, 8 models; Kimi-K2.5 and GPT-5.2 only with Mini-SWE; 3 pairs on a 16-task subset, validated by correlation with full-set scores). Baseline: L0 (framework only, no structural constraints). Held constant: API contract, behavioral test suite, Docker infrastructure, iteration limits per scaffold, prompt template; matched-pair design for marginal constraint effects. Acceptance tests: 291-assertion Postman suite plus static verifiers. Repetitions: 3 trials per task (GPT-5.2 single run on feature tasks). Human intervention: none (automatic re-prompting in OpenHands)

Constraint decay: the nine configurations with L0 A% >50% lose on average 27.48 pp A% from L0 to L3 (worst OpenHands + Qwen3-Coder-Next -45 pp, best OpenHands + MiniMax-M2.5 -17 pp). Marginal effects on A%: PostgreSQL -20.4 ± 2.5 pp, SQLite -16.1 ± 2.6, Clean Architecture -8.8 ± 1.7, SQLAlchemy -4.8 ± 2.6, Sequelize +1.8 ± 2.2. Verifier enforcement changes A% by at most 2.7 pp. Scaffold: OpenHands better for GPT-5-mini and MiniMax-M2.5, worse for Qwen3-Coder-Next. Frameworks (mid-tier configurations): Express 69.2%, Koa 69.8%, Flask 63.6% vs Django 37.4%, FastAPI 34.5%, Hono 25.0% A%; spread 43-69 pp, falling to 16 pp (MiniMax-M2.5) and 21 pp (GPT-5.4). Failures: logic errors 62.1-76.6% of failed runs for three models (GPT-5-mini 50.5% server startup failures); data-layer defects 36.5-60.9% of logic errors (48.4% on average). Feature tasks: only GPT-5.2 exceeds 50% pass@1. Authors: 'the precise effect size should be interpreted with caution'; no significance tests on the decay

Distinguished constraint levels, frameworks and models; A% more stable than pass@1, which authors call noisy. Repeatability: 3 trials per task with standard errors; subset validated against the full set (r 0.948); LLM judge validated (kappa 0.975). Limitations stated by the authors: verifiers are static and pattern-based (possible false positives, false-reject rate <=0.5%); variance of the drop is substantial; feature tasks cannot isolate structural constraints as the cause; single API contract chosen for internal validity; pre-training exposure to the RealWorld specification likely

No separate threats-to-validity section; limitations stated in text and appendices: static, pattern-based verifiers; one API contract (RealWorld Conduit) likely seen in pre-training; effect size uncertain due to variance; subset evaluation for three configurations due to cost; feature tasks only a sanity check. Gaps: agents unreliable for production-grade backends; need structural awareness via retrieval-augmented framework documentation, constraint-oriented planning, or pre-training on convention-heavy codebases; benchmarks should go beyond purely functional checks

Reporting inconsistencies: abstract and contributions give an average loss of 27.28 points (p. 1-2) while Section 5.1 and its takeaway give 27.48 pp (p. 7-8; 27.48 matches Table 2 for the nine configurations); text calls OpenHands + MiniMax-M2.5 'the strongest L3 configuration' with 78.6% A% and 8.3% pass@1 (p. 7), but Mini-SWE + GPT-5.4 has 80.0% A% and 64.6% pass@1 at L3 (Table 2); the verifier comparison gives average decay 26 vs 27 pp (p. 8, 16), a different basis from 27.48. Feature-task repositories use Prisma or SQLAlchemy (Table 10) while the generation ORM constraint for Node is Sequelize. Table 3b and Table 8 layout garbled in text extraction; Table 3b values read in row order. Replication package: https://github.com/francdente/constraint-decay (pipeline, tasks, trajectories, analysis scripts). No pre-registration. Programming languages: Python and JavaScript/TypeScript (Node.js)
